newsitem.title: USA: Dow falls in cautious session, techs extend slump.
newsitem.headline: Dow falls in cautious session, techs extend slump.

text.p: Stocks fell Wednesday as investors turned cautious amid concerns about corporate earnings and braced for the May employment report due on Friday.
Technology stocks led the decline, extending their slump. But in contrast to recent sessions, the market's weakness broadened well beyond the beleaguered tech sector.
The Dow Jones industrial average fell 42.49 points to 7,269.66. In the broader market, declining issues edged gainers, 1,322 to 1,150, on volume of 466.7 million on the New York Stock Exchange.

PepsiCo Inc. became the latest in a string of companies to warn of disappointing earnings, and its stock fell 2-3/8 to 35-7/8. It was the second most active on the NYSE, with more than 8.6 million shares changing hands.

With several recent earnings warnings still reverbating on Wall Street, analysts said it was understandable that investors opted to back off from the market, particularly with the May jobs report due Friday.

"No one is going to want to be a hero in front of the employment number," said Phil Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management. "This market has discounted an awful lot of good news and has no margin for error in earnings or the economy or interest rates."
Selling pressure weighed heaviest on the tech sector, the source of the highest profile earnings warnings.

Intel Corp., which last Friday warned about weaker near-term results, fell 2-1/2 to 142-1/2. That forecast has weighed on the entire computer hardware group due to the nearly universal presence of the giant chip maker's products.

The worries were sufficient to send rumours swirling that personal computer makers were also about to begin issuing warnings. One company, Gateway 2000 Inc. late on Wednesday refuted rumours that it planned such a warning.
Shares in Gateway fell 1/2 to 61-1/2 but slipped as low as 57 during the session. Compaq Computer fell 1-1/2 to 98-1/2 and Dow component International Business Machines fell one to 83-3/8.
"The love-hate relationship with techs continues," said U.S. Clearing Corp. vice president Dick Stein. "Right now, we're in the hate phase."

Analysts said the market probably would stay in a relatively narrow range through Thursday. Friday's jobs report is the last monthly employment report ahead of the meeting of Federal Reserve policy-makers in early July. The central bank's policy-makers held rates steady at their last meeting in May after raising them a quarter point in late March in a bid to ward off inflation.
"The prudent thing to do in the equities market is to raise some cash ahead of a number like this," Orlando said. "That's what we have done."

Among individual issues, Iomega Corp. rose one to 20-1/4 and was the NYSE's most active issue on volume of more than 10 million shares. The company declined to comment after the NYSE requested an explanation for the activity.

H.F. Ahmanson & Co. rose 1-1/4 to 41-1/2 after the company dropped its hostile takeover bid for Great Western Financial Corp. The move clears the way for Great Western's planned merger with Washington Mutual Inc.
Shares in Great Western gained 1-3/8 to 48-3/4. Western Mutual rose 1-1/16 to 54-13/16.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 5.37 points to 840.11. The American Stock Exchange index edged down 1.29 to 607.73.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 2.18 to 440.18. The average price per share lost 21 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues also known as the Wilshire 5000 -- was 7,993.994, down 39.581 or 0.49 percent.
